details:
MISSION CONTROL – Project Details

Tagline: Design. Build. Launch. Operate. Learn.

Project Type: Interactive educational space-mission design and simulation game.

1. Project Overview

MISSION CONTROL is an interactive space exploration and engineering game designed to help students understand how real space missions are planned, designed, launched and operated.

The game combines mission engineering concepts inspired and with simplified rocket-building and flight simulation gameplay inspired by Kerbal Space Program (KSP).

Players take the role of mission commanders and make engineering decisions throughout a complete space mission. They design spacecraft, assemble rockets, manage resources, launch vehicles, reach orbit, deploy satellites and collect scientific data.

The main objective is to make complex aerospace engineering concepts easier to understand through practical gameplay.

2. Problem Statement

Designing a space mission involves balancing multiple engineering requirements, including spacecraft mass, propulsion, power, scientific instruments, communication systems, launch vehicles, budgets and orbital constraints.

Students often learn these concepts separately without understanding how they interact in a real mission.

MISSION CONTROL addresses this challenge by providing an interactive environment where students can experiment with engineering decisions and understand how their choices affect mission success.

3. Main Features

A. Interactive Mission Selection

Players can select from four space exploration missions:

  • Earth Observation: Study Earth's surface, atmosphere, oceans and environmental changes.
  • Moon Exploration: Investigate lunar craters, surface features and environmental conditions.
  • Mars Exploration: Study the Martian surface and atmosphere.
  • Asteroid Exploration: Investigate asteroid composition, characteristics and orbital properties.

Each mission has different objectives, difficulties and engineering requirements.

B. Rocket Building System

Inspired by Kerbal Space Program, the game includes a modular rocket assembly system.

Players can build rockets using components such as:

  • Command capsules.
  • Fuel tanks.
  • Liquid engines.
  • Solid rocket boosters.
  • Decouplers.
  • Fairings.
  • Satellite payloads.
  • Solar panels.
  • Antennas.

Players can attach, remove and configure components, create multiple rocket stages and view their assembled rocket in 3D.

C. Spacecraft Engineering

Players design spacecraft by selecting different systems:

  • Propulsion: Chemical and electric propulsion.
  • Power: Solar panels, batteries and radioisotope power systems.
  • Scientific instruments: Cameras, spectrometers, radar and thermal sensors.
  • Communication: Low-gain and high-gain antennas.
  • Structure: Thermal control, navigation, onboard computers and attitude control.

Every component has properties such as mass, cost, power consumption and scientific contribution.

D. Engineering Calculations

The game automatically calculates important engineering parameters:

  • Total spacecraft and rocket mass.
  • Fuel capacity.
  • Thrust-to-weight ratio (TWR).
  • Delta-v.
  • Power generation and consumption.
  • Payload capacity.
  • Communication capacity.
  • Estimated mission lifetime.

These calculations help players understand the relationship between engineering decisions and mission performance.

All simplified calculations and illustrative values will be labelled as educational estimates.

E. Launch and Flight Simulation

After building the rocket, players proceed to the launchpad.

They experience:

  1. Pre-flight checks.
  2. Countdown.
  3. Engine ignition.
  4. Rocket launch.
  5. Atmospheric ascent.
  6. Stage separation.
  7. Orbital insertion.
  8. Satellite deployment.

Players can control throttle, flight direction and rocket stages while monitoring altitude, velocity, acceleration, fuel and orbital parameters.

F. Mission Operations

After deployment, players manage their spacecraft throughout its mission.

They must monitor:

  • Power consumption.
  • Battery levels.
  • Scientific instruments.
  • Data collection.
  • Communication systems.
  • Data storage.
  • Mission duration.

Random simulated events, such as power shortages, communication failures and instrument malfunctions, challenge players to make decisions and protect their mission.

4. NASA Scientific Data Integration

MISSION CONTROL aims to integrate real scientific information from NASA and JPL.

Potential data sources include:

This integration connects gameplay with real scientific information and helps students explore actual space research.

5. Game Environment and Design

The game begins inside a futuristic mission-control room.

Players start in a commander's chair facing a large observation window with a black hole outside. After selecting Start Mission, the camera moves toward a mission-planning whiteboard.

Following mission selection, players enter the spacecraft and begin their mission.

The interface follows a professional aerospace engineering aesthetic.

Colour palette:

  • Black: #050505
  • Charcoal: #171717
  • Grey: #777777
  • Light grey: #BDBDBD
  • White: #EEEEEE

Three.js will be used for 3D environments, spacecraft, rocket models and camera transitions.

6. Multiplayer and Learning

The planned multiplayer mode supports 2–4 players in local pass-and-play gameplay.

Players can take different responsibilities:

  • Mission Commander.
  • Flight Engineer.
  • Science Officer.
  • Communications Officer.

An integrated learning centre will explain rocket propulsion, staging, orbital mechanics, delta-v, spacecraft power, scientific instruments and satellite communications.

7. Final Mission Report

At the end of each mission, players receive a detailed performance report containing:

  • Mission success or failure.
  • Scientific objectives completed.
  • Data collected and transmitted.
  • Fuel and power efficiency.
  • Engineering performance.
  • Budget usage.
  • Major mission events.
  • Player decisions.
  • Recommendations for improvement.

The scoring system rewards effective engineering decisions, scientific achievements and resource management.

9. Development Roadmap

  1. Inspect and adapt the MARGIN codebase.
  2. Develop mission selection and spacecraft engineering.
  3. Build the modular rocket assembly system.
  4. Implement engineering calculations.
  5. Develop launch, staging and flight simulation.
  6. Implement Earth-orbit insertion and satellite deployment.
  7. Add mission operations and NASA data integration.
  8. Expand to Moon, Mars and asteroid missions.
  9. Add multiplayer and educational tutorials.
  10. Test and improve the complete experience.

10. Expected Impact

MISSION CONTROL aims to transform space engineering education from passive learning into interactive experimentation.

Students will understand that adding fuel increases mass, powerful instruments consume more energy, communication systems affect scientific data delivery and reaching orbit requires more than simply gaining altitude.

MISSION CONTROL makes space-mission engineering interactive, understandable and engaging by allowing students to experience the complete journey from mission design to scientific discovery.
